case_name: Split Vision Eyewear Inc. v. The Economical Insurance Group
text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Split Vision Eyewear Inc. v. The
Economical Insurance Group,

2010 BCSC 396

Date: 20100209

Docket:
S093983

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Split Vision Eyewear Inc.

Plaintiff

And

The Economical Insurance Group,
Economical Mutual Insurance Company

and Lloyd’s of London Limited

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Walker

Oral Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

R.A. Jarvis

Counsel for the Defendants:

D.K.
Plunkett

A. Maltas

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

February 9, 2010

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

February 9, 2010

THE
COURT:

Introduction

[
1
]

The applications brought in this case raise the
following issues:

(a)       who bears the onus of proving whether the defendant
seeking an order for security for costs to be posted has, or does not have, an arguable
defence;

(b)       the nature of the evidence required by the Court to
determine whether an arguable defence has been shown; and

(c)        whether a solicitor, or legal professional from the law
firm on his behalf, who swears an affidavit on behalf of a client that not only
concerns but represents a matter of substance – in this case, the nature of the
evidence purporting to demonstrate an arguable defence – results in a waiver of
solicitor/client privilege.

[
2
]

Two applications have been argued before me:

(a)       an application brought on behalf of the defendants,
pursuant to
s. 236
of the
Business Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57
for the following orders:

(i)         the plaintiff be required to post security for costs of
the defendants within 14 days, or such other time period as ordered by the
court;

(ii)        the amount of the security be set by the court; and,

(iii)       the plaintiff's action be stayed pending the posting of
such security;

and,

(b)       an application brought on behalf of the plaintiff for the
following orders:

(i)         the defendants produce the documents referred to as
“evidence” in paras. 10 and 11 of the affidavit of Ms. Natasha Haines,
a legal assistant employed at the law firm of Whitelaw Twining, sworn November
19, 2009;

(ii)         the defendants produce for inspection and copying the
documents listed in Part 3 of the defendants' list of documents;  and,

(iii)       promptly thereafter Ms. Haines be produced for
cross-examination on her affidavit.

[
3
]

The defendants' application for a “guillotine”
order, i.e., that the plaintiff's action be dismissed without further
application should the plaintiff fail to post security, has been abandoned.

Facts
Underlying the Applications

[
4
]

The plaintiff, Split Vision Eyewear, distributes
eyewear.  Its claim against the insurers is for an alleged breach of insurance
policy WIC044256, as a result of their failure to pay for loss arising from the
theft of the plaintiff's eyewear inventory said to have occurred in the early
hours of June 1, 2008.

[
5
]

At the time of the alleged theft, the plaintiff
was the distributor of high quality, unique eyewear imported directly from
Europe.  The plaintiff was the exclusive distributor of eyewear manufactured by
OPO Design Sweden AB.  The product name has been referred to on this
application as “X-ICE” and “X-IDE”.  In addition, the plaintiff was a
distributor of high-end Italian eyewear known as “Pollini”.

[
6
]

At the time of the alleged theft, the plaintiff
held an insurance policy subscribed to by the defendant insurers.

[
7
]

The principals of the plaintiff are Sheila Helgason
and Helgi Helgason.  At all material times, the plaintiff's inventory was
maintained and stored in a two-car garage attached to Mr. and Mrs. Helgason's
home located at 1894-165A Street in Surrey, British Columbia.

[
8
]

In her affidavit sworn December 2, 2009, Ms.
Helgason deposes, in paras. 3 to 11, about the plaintiff’s business and the
effect of the loss:

3.  In creating Split Vision, my business
partner, Helgi Helgason, and I had invested a considerable amount of time and
effort into building the business and reputation of this company by attending
various trade shows in U.S. cities, developing a training program for sales
representatives, establishing contracts with other businesses, and advertising
regularly in optical trade magazines.  We have travelled extensively and have
been taking on new collections as our reputation grew in the market.  Our
potential for growth was significant such that we began to look for an investor
or partner.  We have been committed to developing Split Vision into a successful
business.

4.  I am experienced in the sales industry
as I have been working in the optical industry since 1992 and I was one of the
very first sales representatives hired by Marchon Eyewear in Canada.  I also
was one of Marchon Eyewear's top sales representatives in Canada.

5.  Prior to the theft of the designer eyewear
on June 1, 2008 from 1894-165 A Street, Surrey, British Columbia, Split Vision
maintained consistent growth in gross sales.  The gross sales for Split Vision
in 2005 from both U.S. and Canadian sales was $508,648.00.  In 2006, this
amount was $862,872.90.  For 2007, the projected sales according to the
Business Plan was $1,925,000.00 and the total gross sales for this year was
$1,176,663.00.

6.  Split Vision's gross sales for 2008 ought
to have exceeded the amount of $1,176,663.00 but the total gross sales only
amounted to $790,109.44.  In January 2008 we had our collections, sales team,
and inside sales staff in place.  We were expecting to have a profitable year.
From January to May 2008, our gross income was the highest it has been since
previous years.

7.  After June 2008, we initially felt
confident that we would be able to rebuild our business from the payout from
our insurance policy.  However, as time passed, I was concerned because our
insurers were not forthcoming in providing coverage for our loss of inventory.
I was concerned about going into months in which sales are typically strong
without sufficient stock.  Typically, in our summer and winter months we have
sales for older merchandise which allows us to keep the sales volume moving.
However, as a lot of the stock was not replaced, it impacted our business
greatly.  I kept hoping that the insurers would assist us financially even with
an advance but this never happened.

8.  I had also hoped to rebuild Split
Vision's business by working with the suppliers from Europe to attempt to get
the product as quickly as possible but this was a challenge as they did not
want to supply product to us without prepayment.  I felt let down that Split
Vision could not reach its goals.  We were distracted by the issues surrounding
the denial of coverage for our loss by the insurers which prevented us from
focusing all our efforts on building the business.

9.  Eventually, our European suppliers also
grew frustrated with us because they attempted to send us product which we were
not able to repay.  Receiving insurance funds in a timely way would have
alleviated our difficulties by allowing us to rebuild our inventory and pay
suppliers.  Although we have maintained good business relations with OPO Design
Sweden AB, we have been abandoned by at least one other long-standing supplier
who has found a new distributor.

10.  This time was difficult for me due to
the humiliation we had to experience before our suppliers, account holders, and
others in the industry who became aware that we were being investigated.  Split
Vision had a reputation as a great distributor and we were very respected in
our business.

11.  We have
since moved from our previous business address and we no longer stock eye
frames as we do not want to experience anything like this again.  Our
relationship with our supplie[r]s has also changed as we no longer distribute
but the suppliers now ship directly to our accounts.  Our suppliers also pay us
directly.

[
9
]

The defendants (“insurers”) claim that there was
no theft.  They allege that the inventory of eye glasses said to have been
stolen was in fact removed from the premises prior to June 1, 2008, by either or
both of the Helgasons or by a person or persons acting on their behalf.

[
10
]

The insurers' evidence is set out in Ms. Haines'
affidavit sworn November 19, 2009.  She deposes at paras. 1, 10, 11, and 12:

1.         I am
a legal assistant with Whitelaw Twining Law Corporation, solicitors for the Defendants
and have personal knowledge of the facts hereinafter deposed to, save and
except where the same are stated to be on information and belief, and where so
stated, I verily believe them to be true.

10.       I am
informed by Mr. William G. Neen, the lawyer at Whitelaw Twining Law Corporation
having conduct of the defence of the action, that liability is at issue in this
case and there is a meritorious defence for the Defendants.  The Defendants
will lead evidence to show that the Plaintiff and the Plaintiff's principals
are responsible for any damages suffered by the plaintiff and that the action
has been fraudulently brought by the Plaintiff and the Plaintiff's principals
for the purpose of committing insurance fraud against the defendants.  The
Defendants will show that the Plaintiff and its principals:

(a)        arranged the alleged theft and disposal of the eye glass
inventory themselves;

(b)        misled the Defendants on the value of the property for
the purpose of reducing the amount they would have to pay as co-insureds; and

(c)        brought the current action in
abuse of the Court's process.

11.       I am informed by Mr. Neen that the evidence of fraud on
the part of the Plaintiff includes:

(a)        the alleged thief or thieves would had to have had
detailed knowledge of the premises from which the eyeglass inventory was taken;

(b)        the alleged thief or thieves would had to have had
knowledge that the eyeglass inventory had been placed in garbage bags the
previous day;

(c)        the alleged thief or thieves would had to have been able
to break into the premises and get away with the eyeglass inventory without
triggering a motion sensor on the premises;

(d)        the alleged theft took place within a time span of less
than 30 seconds;

(e)        nothing was heard by at least three adults and three dogs
in the premises at the time of the alleged theft; and

(f)         the evening prior to the alleged theft, two garbage bags
of eyeglass inventory matching the description of the loss claimed were found
in a garbage bin.

12.       I am
informed by Mr. Neen that the Defendants deny the allegations raised by the Plaintiff
and will argue at trial that they have fulfilled all of their contractual
obligations under the Policy and have acted in the utmost good faith.

[
11
]

In para. 13, Ms. Haines deposes as to the anticipated
costs (of the action) that relate to the insurers' application for the posting
of security:

I am informed
that the anticipated costs should these Defendants be successful at trial are
$51,992.05.  Attached and marked as Exhibit “Contract” is a true copy of a
draft prospective Bill of Costs.

[
12
]

The insurers formally denied coverage on October
15, 2008.  The basis of the denial is set out in correspondence signed by Mr.
Neen and addressed to the solicitor that was representing the plaintiff at the
time, Mr. Gordon Hilliker, Q.C.  In that correspondence, Mr. Neen identified
the facts underlying the insurers’ coverage denial.  He wrote:

We confirm receipt of the Proof of Loss
dated August 21, 2008 which was submitted claiming a loss of $164,398.83 less
$1,000 deductible relating to the replacement costs of your client's stock
which is claimed to have been stolen.

We understand that your client claims that,
at approximately 2:45 a.m. on June 1, 2008, a break and enter occurred to its
premises at which time a quantity of its stock of eyeglass wear was taken from
the garage area used as part of the business premises.  The eyeglass wear was
apparently contained in at least 2 plastic garbage bags at the time of the
alleged theft and it is those garbage bags that were stolen.

Investigation into the circumstances of the
alleged theft has concluded that, for such a theft to have occurred, the thief
or thieves would have had to have detailed knowledge of the premises as well as
the fact that the stock being targeted had, the day before, been placed into
garbage bags.  Further, the thieves would have to have been able to break into
the house and get away with the garbage bags of stock without triggering the
motion sensor located in the garage all within a space of time under 30
seconds.  Compounded with that is the fact that the premises was occupied at
the time by at least 3 adults and 3 dogs and none of those heard anything
unusual other than the perimeter alarm or alarm company telephoning the home.

These facts in themselves suggest the
implausibility of a theft taking place as alleged, however, when combined with
the fact that an independent witness observed 2 garbage bags of eyeglasses
being apparently disposed of the evening prior to the alleged theft, in the
Insurers’ view, there is little doubt that the Insured is not being honest in
its claim of a theft of stock as stated in the Proof of Loss.

In submitting the claim, you sent a letter
dated August 25, 2008 in which your client has represented that a large portion
of stock that was in its possession, was not, in fact ‘stock’ for the purposes
of calculating the effect of the coinsurance provisions.  This is in spite of
the fact that, until the date of loss, those items were apparently included in
the perpetual inventory maintained by your client for all stock and treated as
inventory on your client's books.

You are aware of
the relation between the Insurers and the Insured is one of utmost good faith
and requires honesty in dealings with one another.

You are also
aware that the Policy provides as follows: ...

At that point,
Mr. Neen referred to para. 7, which speaks of the “perils” excluded in the
policy.  It reads:

This form does not cover any
loss or damage:

...

k.          by any dishonest act on your
part or any other party of interest, employees or your agents, or any person to
whom the property may be entrusted (bailees for hire excepted) but this
exclusion does not apply to physical damage caused directly by your employees
which results from a peril insured against and not otherwise excluded under
this Part.

[
13
]

Mr. Neen then went on to say:

As a result of
the above facts, we are instructed to advise you that the insurers are of the
opinion that, to your client's knowledge, it did not, in fact, suffer a theft
as claimed and, in calculating the amount of the claim submitted has contrived
to falsely reduce the amount of its inventory of stock in an effort to reduce
the effect of the co-insurance penalty and, in furtherance of such connivance,
has submitted a willfully false statement in its Proof of Loss, the effect of
which vitiates the claim.  Accordingly, we are instructed to advise you that
this claim is being denied by the Insurers.

[
14
]

The connivance issue, which concerns an alleged
false reduction in the amount of the inventory, was not argued on this
application as a basis for posting security for costs.

[
15
]

At the hearing of this application the insurers
advanced the following evidence to support the coverage denial:

(a)       the recorded witness statement of an independent witness made
to an employee of one of the insurers, the Economical Insurance Company;

(b)       evidence of the plaintiff's purported financial
difficulties prior to the alleged theft (which did not form any basis for the
insurers’ coverage denial set out in Mr. Neen’s correspondence); and

(c)        a report prepared by Peter Senez of Senez Reed Calder
(forensic engineers) dated September 2, 2008, that sets out,
inter alia
,
the route by which the reported thieves would have to follow to carry out the
theft, the location of the alarm sensors in the Helgasons’ home, and the
limited amount of time available to commit the theft before the alarm was
activated.

[
16
]

At p. 5 of his report, Mr. Senez opined:

To accomplish the
above tasks within the time-frames indicated on the alarm monitoring report
would likely require specialized knowledge of the house.  It is unclear why a
perpetrator would use tools to extensively force the exterior door and then not
use tools to force the interior door.  Had the deadbolt been properly engaged,
it would have been extremely difficult to remove the door in the manner
described above.

[
17
]

The Helgasons response to the insurers’
allegations is contained in their respective affidavits.

[
18
]

Sheila Helgason deposed, in her affidavit sworn
December 2, 2009, at paras. 14 to 16 and 19:

14.       The Defendants did disclose a
redacted copy of a witness statement that states that a witness saw a man
disposing of two garbage bags full of glasses.  We are not aware of the
identity of both of these individuals, the date, and location on which this
would have occurred.  We followed up on this with the Defendants' claims
adjuster and there are discrepancies between our situation and what is
described in that statement.  For example, of the two bags discovered in a bin
by the witness only 5 frames of potentially 50 frames were ones Split Vision
carried and several of these frames were not even reported missing by us.  A
further discrepancy relates to the amount of frames found in the bins which
were around 50 or so compared to the thousands that were stolen from Split
Vision.

15.       I do not agree with paragraph 11
of Ms. Haines' Affidavit that the thieves would have had to have knowledge of
the premises, that they had to act in less than 30 seconds, or that the
eyeglass inventory had to be placed in bags the previous day.  I do not think
this has to be the case as the Defendants allege.  We have stacked inventory
fairly high in the past which may have obstructed the motion sensors.  We were
all asleep with our dogs at the time of the theft and we did not hear
anything.  The Defendants ought to provide more details about these
allegations.

16.       I am very concerned that the
Defendants' upcoming Application for Security for Costs will be a further
obstacle in overcoming this episode which began in June 2008.  It is not fair
that we are being placed in the position to provide funds to the Defendants
when we have experienced harm to our finances and reputations as a result of
their inaction.

...

19.       If
the court requires Split Vision to post security for costs I do not know where
we will get the funds to do that.  If the amount requested is as substantial as
the amount shown in the defence application materials ($50,000) it is almost
certain that Split Vision will not be able to pursue what I know to be a
meritorious claim against the defendants.

[
19
]

In her further affidavit sworn December 15,
2009, Ms. Helgason deposed in paras. 4 and 5:

4.         Attached as
Exhibit
"C"
is a true copy of the ADT Account History for the Split
Vision premises from June 1, 2008 to June 2, 2008.  The ADT record demonstrates
that from the time of the forced entry at the patio door (2:46:46 a.m.) to the
time that the laundry room door sensor was triggered (2:47:21 a.m.), it took 35
seconds.  The alarm did go off, ADT called me and ADT did contact the police.
It took 3 minutes and 41 seconds from the time that the patio door was opened
to the time that ADT cleared the alarm.

5.         Attached
and marked
Exhibit "D"
is Defendants' document no. 79, a true
copy of an email from Bob Convey to Sarah Gabl dated July 14, 2008 which
summarizes their witness statements.  Helgi Helgason's date of birth is
December 23, 1957,
making him 52 years of age
.                        [emphasis
added]

[
20
]

The third affidavit is from Helgi Helgason. It
was sworn December 2, 2009.  At paras. 2 to 13, he deposed:

2.         I have extensive experience in
the optical industry, over 18 years.  Prior to creating Split Vision with my
partner, Sheila Helgason ("Sheila"), I worked as a sales
representative for Marchon Eyewear and did become one of the company's top sale
representatives for the entire company worldwide.

3.         In 2005 I decided to begin a
business with Sheila and create a niche market in North America for high-end,
European eyewear.  We wanted to build an image for our company as a distributor
providing the best customer service, offering unique and fashionable eyewear
from Europe.

4.         I researched and collected
contacts from various suppliers located in Europe.  I maintained contact with
these suppliers and eventually developed relationships with them whereby I
would distribute their eyewear collections.  I was focused on developing Split
Vision into a successful company and our gross sales reflect our hard work in
expanding our business.  Since 2005, Split Vision has increased its sales each
year with the exception of 2008.

5.         On June 1, 2008 there was a theft
of eye-frames from Split Vision.  The Defendants denied insurance coverage to
us despite repeated requests for payment and assistance.  The Defendants began
to suggest that the theft did not occur and that we were responsible for our
loss.  The theft and the denial of coverage for our loss negatively affected
our business and our future in the industry in that we suffered financial loss,
personal stress, and damage to our reputation.

6.         In response to the allegation of
the evidence of fraud in Ms. Haines' Affidavit sworn on November 19, 2009,
neither Split Vision nor I as the co- owner of Split Vision have engaged in any
fraud surrounding the theft of eye frames on June 1, 2008 from 1894-165 A
Street, Surrey, British Columbia.    Split Vision was developing its business
such that in 2007 our gross sales were $1,176,663.00 and we expected to exceed
this amount for 2008.  Our gross sales for 2008 were $790,109.44.

7.         In August 2008, Split Vision
requested an advance from the Defendants' claims adjuster but this was
refused.  We attempted to replace the stolen property by requesting the
suppliers to send product replacement without requiring pre-payment but this
was difficult to do once the supplier realized that Split Vision was under
investigation by the insurance companies for fraud.  We eventually lost one of
our long-time and oldest suppliers of eye-frames as well as damaged our
reputation in the industry.

8.          In response to Mr. Geluch's Affidavit
sworn on November 19, 2009, Split Vision has encountered a few unfortunate
business experiences in its expansion into the Canadian business market.  Split
Vision has contract disputes with Liquid Capital Exchange Corp. ("Liquid
Capital"), Integrated Office Systems Inc. ("Integrated"), and
Irwin Commercial Finance Canada Corporation ("Irwin").  Split Vision
is currently defending claims by these companies in the court system.  This in
no way, however, reflects Split Vision's potential for growth but are
contractual disagreements between Split Vision and others.

9.         Due to the damage to Split
Vision's reputation, I decided to incorporate two companies with Sheila, Helmac
Eyewear Ltd. and Stylish Eyewear Ltd.  We created these companies in order to
carry on our business and seek other brands to sell.  We were concerned that we
would lose the brands that we had because after the theft we could not continue
to make regular payments to our existing suppliers.  This was an attempt to
build our reputation again from scratch.

10.       Split Vision currently does not
have assets.  The 2008 Annual Report was filed; however, the 2009 Annual Report
was not filed but will be filed.

11.       In response to Ms. Haines'
Affidavit, paragraph 5, the property located at 11117-159th Street belongs to
my father.  I am not the owner of this property.  I do not own the property.  I
had to sell my assets in order to start the eye frames business.

12.       Due to our fragile position in the
industry and the difficult circumstances we have had to face since the theft and
the denial of coverage by the Defendants, the Defendants ought not to be able
to benefit from our weak financial circumstance by arguing that we are not in a
position to post security when the reason we have experienced financial
difficulty is because of the theft and their denial of insurance coverage.
This is another obstacle that is causing unnecessary stress on both me and my
partner professionally and personally.

13.       If
the court requires Split Vision to post security for costs I do not know where
we will get the funds to do that.  If the amount requested is as substantial as
the amount shown in the defence application materials ($50,000) it is almost
certain that Split Vision will not be able to pursue what I know to be a
meritorious claim against the defendants.

[
21
]

The witness statement obtained for the insurers
was not provided to the plaintiff until November 5, 2008, and when it was, the
witness' name was redacted.  The witness' name was ultimately provided on
December 7 or 8, 2009, when the insurers’ delivered their list of documents
after being served with an application by counsel for the plaintiff seeking and
order for document production.

[
22
]

The report prepared by Mr. Senez was
commissioned before the insurers denied coverage, but was not disclosed to the
plaintiff until the insurers' list of documents was delivered on December 7 or
8, 2009.

[
23
]

After the insurers' denial of coverage was
communicated to the plaintiff, and prior to the production of the redacted
witness statement, Mr. Hilliker wrote to Mr. Neen requesting information
from the insurers (including witness statements) as to the manner in which the
ten eyeglass frames the insurers said were part of the plaintiff's inventory
had come into the their possession.  On November 4, 2008, Mr. Hilliker
wrote in an e-mail to Mr. Neen:

Mr. Neen:

My clients have viewed the 10 frames that
are in your client’s possession.  I am advised that 4 out of the 10 do not
match the description of the frames that were reported stolen.  How do you or
your clients account for this fact?

I reiterate my
request that you provide us with all of the information that your clients have
concerning the manner in which these 10 frames came into their possession.
This request includes any witness statements or interview notes.  On what
possible basis can the insurers, acting in good faith, refuse to provide this
information to us?

[
24
]

Mr. Neen responded, advising that while he was
prepared to provide a redacted copy of a witness statement he would not
recommend production of any further information by the insurers absent
litigation.  On November 4, 2008, he wrote the following to Mr. Hilliker:

Hi Gordon,

I am interested to see that your clients
admit that at least 6 pairs of glasses fit the description of those they allege
were stolen.  I have no specific explanation for why it is that they say the
other 4 do not fit but, I will certainly be looking into that if this matter
progresses.  One potential explanation is that the itemization of the items
that were put in the bags and alleged to be stolen was incorrect.

On the Witness statement you have asked for,
I am advised that the witness does not want to have the identity disclosed and does
not want to speak with you or your clients but is prepared to have the
statement given to you with any identifying comments taken out.  I am in the
process of doing that and should have that to you tomorrow.

Beyond
production of the above, I am not inclined to recommend the further production
of information as it is my view that you have the basis for the Insurers'
denial in sufficient detail to allow your client to take whatever steps it
deems appropriate in the circumstances.  Any further production will be made in
accordance with the Rules of Court, at which time both parties will have equal
rights of discovery.

I hope to be in
touch again tomorrow with the redacted Witness Statement.

[
25
]

Mr. Hilliker responded, advising that the
plaintiff had no choice but to commence litigation.  He wrote to Mr. Neen on
November 7, 2008 stating:

Bill:

I’m a bit puzzled by your reference to “the
items that were put in the bags and alleged to be stolen".  The claim is
for over 3000 frames that are alleged to have been stolen.  It is not claimed
that they were all in bags.  There was product in boxes.

As for the 6 recovered frames that match the
description of the product stolen, I am sure that you understand that there are
no serial numbers on individual frames. So all that can be said is that a frame
of that type was stolen in the break-in.

I have now received and reviewed the
redacted witness statement.  As you might well expect, there are a number of
questions that we have for this witness.  It is apparent that there are other
witnesses as well who could be expected to have information pertaining to the recovered
product.

The theory that
the insurers are advancing in this case seems quite bizarre to me.  But, given
the refusal of the insurers to provide us with the names of witnesses as well
as their refusal to provide us with all of the information they relied upon in
denying this claim, the insureds are left with no option except to commence
litigation.

[
26
]

Although that witness statement was produced,
with the name of the witness removed, the insurers did not produce any further
documentation or information until well after the lawsuit was commenced on May
29, 2009, and then only after the plaintiff's application to compel production
of documents was served upon them in late November 2009.  I was advised by
counsel during the hearing of the instant applications that the position taken
by the insurers prior to the plaintiff’s production application was that they,
the insurers, should not be put to the expense of producing a list of documents
until after their security for costs application was heard.  The plaintiff did
not agree and served its application.  The insurers' list of documents was then
delivered on December 7 or 8, 2009.

[
27
]

Thus, the name of the witness was first
identified to the plaintiff by the insurers in December 2009.  Efforts by
counsel for the plaintiff to speak with that witness have been unsuccessful as
the witness is not returning his telephone calls or responding to messages.

[
28
]

The witness statement was taken by an employee
of the Economical Insurance Company on July 25, 2008.  It was put into evidence
as an exhibit to a further affidavit sworn by Ms. Haines.  It is not a sworn
statement.  There is no affidavit from that insurer’s employee who took the
statement, Mr. Convey, confirming that the information in the statement was
provided to him by the witness,  nor is there an explanation of the
circumstances in which the statement was taken.  In fact, even though other
evidence in the chambers record shows that Mr. Convey had a previous
conversation with the witness in May 2008, there is no information, let alone
evidence, showing what they discussed.  As well, evidence in the chambers
record shows that the witness subsequently met with an R.C.M.P. officer in July
or August 2000.  The witness appears, at that time, to have resiled from his
ability to identify the individual carrying what he said were black garbage
bags.

[
29
]

The essence of the information provided by the
witness to Mr. Convey on July 25, 2008 is as follows:

(a)       while on a
break from his shift at a restaurant in Surrey, the witness was eating in the

The
Application for Security for Costs

The
law – general principles:

[
40
]

Section 236
of the
Business Corporations Act
,
S.B.C., 2002, c. 57, provides courts with the jurisdiction to order the posting
of security if it appears that a plaintiff corporation will not be able to pay
the costs of the defendant if the defendant is successful in the defence.  The court
may also order a stay of all legal proceedings until security is posted.

[
41
]

In the case of a personal plaintiff, the basic
rule is that a natural person should not be barred from having his day in court
because of impecuniosity, so that the court's power to require security to be
posted should be exercised with restraint.  There is no such rule in the case
of a limited company.

[
42
]

Mr. Justice Ehrcke discussed the rationale for a
different rule for limited companies.  In
Beasse v. Holness
,
2006 BCSC
1265
, he quoted, at para. 14, from
Pearson v. Naydler
,
[1977] 3 All E.R.
531 at p. 535
:

In the case of
a limited company, there is no basic rule conferring immunity from any
liability to give security for costs.  The basic rule is the opposite; s. 447
applies to all limited companies, and subjects them all to the liability to
give security for costs. The whole concept of the section is contrary to the
rule developed by the cases that poverty is not to be made a bar to bringing an
action.  There is nothing in the statutory language (the substance of which
goes back at least as far as the
Companies Act
1862 s. 69) to indicate
that there are any exceptions to what is laid down as a broad and general rule
for all limited companies.  Nor is it surprising that there should be such a
rule. A man may bring into being as many limited companies as he wishes, with
the privilege of limited liability, and s. 447 provides some protection for the
community against litigious abuses by artificial persons manipulated by natural
persons.  One should be as slow to whittle away this protection as one should
be to whittle away a natural persons’ [sic] right to litigate despite poverty.

[
43
]

The purpose of an order for security for costs
is discussed in the 1993 Court of Appeal decision in
Fat Mel's Restaurant
Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.
, (1993)
1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (2d)
231.  At para. 19, Madam Justice Proudfoot quoted from the words of Spencer J.
in the 1991 decision of
Island Research & Development Corp. v. Boeing
Co.
,
1991 CanLII 598 (BC SC)
, [1991] B.C.J. No. 12 (Q.L.):

The purpose of
security for costs is to protect a defendant from the likelihood that in the
event of its success it will be unable to recover its costs from the plaintiff.
The plaintiff is not to be permitted a free ride on an unlikely claim at the
defendants’ expense.  The factors to be considered in achieving a just balance
between the defendants’ right to protection and the plaintiffs’ right to
advance a potential claim for adjudication include the chance of the claim's
success, the anticipated level of cost in conducting the action and the
prospect of the plaintiffs ever having assets from which to pay the defendants'
costs if the claim fails.

[
44
]

At para. 19 of
Fat Mel's
, the Court of
Appeal elaborated on the purpose of security for costs, emphasizing that the
order is discretionary and that the burden of proof lies on the defendant.

[
45
]

In the 1997 Court of Appeal decision of
Kropp
v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.
, (1997)
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252, Finch J.A.
(as he then was), writing for the court, referred (at para. 17) to the
following principles outlined by the English Court of Appeal in
Keary
Development v. Tarmac Construction
,
[1995] 3 All E.R. 534
, as a “useful
guide”:

1.  The court has a complete discretion
whether to order security, and will act in light of all the relevant
circumstances;

2.  The possibility or probability that the
plaintiff company will be deterred from pursuing its claim is not, without more,
sufficient reason for not ordering security;

3.  The court must attempt to balance
injustices arising from use of security as an instrument of oppression to
stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of impecuniosity as a means
of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the other;

4.  The court may have regard to the merits
of the action, but should avoid going into detail on the merits unless success
or failure appears obvious;

5.  The court can order any amount of
security up to the full amount claimed, as long as the amount is more than
nominal;

6.  Before the court refuses to order
security on the ground that it would unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court
must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it is probable that the claim
would be stifled; and

7.  The
lateness of the application for security is a circumstance which can properly
be taken into account.

[
46
]

The factors to be considered on an application
for security for costs respecting a corporate plaintiff were laid out by Mr.
Justice Romilly in
Citizens For Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish
Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.) at para.14.  There are four
factors:

1.  Does it appear that the plaintiff
company will be unable to pay the defendants' costs if the action fails?

2.  If so, has the plaintiff shown that it
has exigible assets of sufficient value to satisfy an award of costs?

3.  Is the court satisfied that the
defendants have an arguable defence to present?

4.  Would an
order for costs visit undue hardship on the plaintiff such that it would prevent
the plaintiff's case from being heard?

The same point was made in
Old Mac's
Pty. Ltd. v. Cavallo Horse & Rider Inc.
,
2007 BCSC 726
at para.
47
.

[
47
]

The plaintiff admits that it will not be able to
pay the insurers' costs if the action fails and also admits that it lacks
exigible assets to satisfy an award of costs.  Thus the inquiry on the
defendants' application concerns factors 3 and 4 as outlined in
Citizens for
Foreign Aid Reform
: i.e., do the defendants have an arguable defence to
present, and, would an order for costs visit undue hardship on the plaintiff
such that it would prevent the plaintiff's case from being heard?

Arguable
Defence:

[
48
]

What evidence is required in relation to the
issue of arguable defence and who bears the onus of proof?  The following cases
show that the nature of the evidence considered on a security for costs
application is context specific, and includes the nature of the case as well as
what stage the proceedings are at when the application is brought.

[
49
]

In
Beasse
, Mr. Justice Ehrcke remarked at
para. 8 that it was “not necessary ... for the defendants to establish that
they will inevitably or even likely succeed.  All that is required is that they
have a
bona fide
defence which arguably may succeed”.  In determining whether
the test had been met by the defendants, Ehrcke J. examined, albeit in a
summary way, the merits of the plaintiff's allegations and the defendant’s
response (the latter contained in an affidavit sworn by one of the defendant’s
solicitors in a solicitor’s malpractice action).  He also considered the
submissions of counsel.

[
50
]

In
Canadian Star Development Corp. v. 0712276
B.C. Ltd.
,
2008 BCSC 61
, Master Scarth considered, at the very early stage
of proceeding, where the defendant had filed a pro forma statement of defence,
the defendant's position set out in a letter from counsel for the corporate
defendant attached to an affidavit.

[
51
]

In
International Nesmont Industrial Corp. v.
Coopers & Lybrand,

[1998] B.C.J. No. 2626 (S.C.)
, Smith J. (as he then
was) made his determination based on the "significant" issues of law
and fact raised in the pleadings, and concluded, at para. 11:  “I am not
persuaded the defendants do not have an arguable case”.

[
52
]

In
New Westminster Contracting Ltd. v. Nagina
Property Ltd.
,
2007 BCSC 1561
, Daphne Smith J. (as she then was) looked,

inter alia
, at the positions in the pleadings since the case was at the
very early stages of the proceedings.

[
53
]

It is not clear in
Island Research and
Development Corp.
what evidence Mr. Justice Spencer considered, at p.
4, in reaching his conclusion, although it is clear that he considered, at the
very early stage of the proceedings, before discoveries have been held:

...[evidence] which
might clarify the issues that will proceed to trial, [the case had the
potential to be] a long and complex matter, both in the pre trial stages and at
trial [where] much will apparently turn on the credibility of the various
actors who played parts in the negotiations between the first three plaintiffs
and the Boeing group...

[
54
]

In
Kropp
,
the Court of Appeal noted, at
para. 2, that:

The learned
chambers judge found that both sides to the dispute had meritorious positions,
and that ultimate success or failure in the law suit would likely turn on
questions of credibility which she could not decide on the material before
her.  She refused an order for security for costs against Mr. Kropp, the
principal shareholder of his co-plaintiff, and no appeal is taken against that
part of her order.  The learned chambers judge found that the plaintiffs would
be unable to prosecute their claim if she were to grant an order for security
for costs against the corporate plaintiff.  This appeal depends in large part
upon whether the affidavit evidence supports that finding. There are also questions
concerning the correct principles to apply in exercising the discretionary
power found in s.229 of the
Company Act
[R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 59].

[
55
]

Kropp
involved a
claim for,
inter alia
, damages for wrongful termination of a management
and development contract relating to the Swaneset Golf Course.  Although the
appeal was allowed in relation to the hardship issue (i.e., the plaintiff would
be prevented from pursuing its claim due to impecuniosity), the Court of Appeal
concluded that the chambers judge did not err in her assessment of the
evidence.  At para. 19, Finch J.A. said:

It cannot be
said that she erred in finding the merits equally balanced where the case is
one which will ultimately depend on findings of credibility.

[
56
]

In
Old Mac's Pty. Ltd.
, Dickson J. seems
to have considered the direct evidence of parties before concluding that the
plaintiff's claim did not appear to be strong against the defendant, such that
the defendant had an arguable defence.

[
57
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
,
Romilly J. discussed both the nature of the evidence required and the relative
burdens on the plaintiff and the defendant.  At para. 19, Romilly J. said, “it
must be evident on the record before the Court that the defendant does not have
an arguable defence” for the plaintiff to avoid an order for costs:  the judge
must be satisfied the defence is “
bona fide”
.  See also
Ruko of
Canada Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce

(1991), 49 C.P.C. (2d)
105 (B.C.S.C.)
.

[
58
]

Read together, the remarks of Romilly J.
expressed in paras. 14, 20, and 23, show that he viewed the onus on the parties
as bilateral.  The onus falls first on the defendant.  The defendants, he said,
do not need to show that they will ultimately prevail, "but merely that
they have a reasonable defence to the plaintiff's claim...”.  Once that onus is
met by the defendants, an onus falls upon the plaintiff to establish that it
can satisfy the defendant’s costs or failing that, to respond with evidence to
establish that the defendants have no arguable case, or that the order for
security will stifle the action.

[
59
]

The Court took the same view of the onus in
Spartans
Canadian Football Association of BC v. McAvoy
,
2001 BCSC 1305
at para.
12
:
“it is well established that the onus is on the applicant to show that the plaintiff
will not likely be able to pay costs if they are awarded against it.  Once that
onus has been met, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to establish that there
is no arguable defence”.

[
60
]

The enquiry does not stop there, however.  In
Spartans
Canadian Football
Association
, Quijano J. dealt with the question of the
definition of “arguable defence”.  At para.15, she said:

What is meant by "an arguable
defence" on an application such as this, where to find that there is an
arguable defence could result in the plaintiff's claims being stifled?  To
constitute an arguable defence there must be
some evidence
, which if
believed, would give the defendant a defence to the claims being made against
him.  In the circumstances of this case that evidence must consist of something
more than the defendant's bare denial.

[emphasis
added]

[
61
]

None of the other cases discuss the nature or
parameters of the evidence required to show either a “reasonable defence” or
the lack of an arguable defence.

[
62
]

No decision of the Court of Appeal has been
cited to me in respect of the notion that the onus shifts to the plaintiff to
prove what is in essence a negative proposition – that the defendant lacks an
arguable case or defence.

[
63
]

Apart from
Citizens for Foreign Aid
and
Spartans
Canadian Football Association
, no case from this Court has been cited to me
dealing with the question of onus in relation to the issue of “no arguable
defence”.

[
64
]

The Court of Appeal's decision in
Kropp
,
decided in 1997, approximately two years before
Citizens

for Foreign
Aid
and four years prior to
Spartans Canadian Football Association
,
did not speak of onus in relation to this issue.  Instead, the Court of Appeal
remarked upon three things: (a) that the chambers judge looked at the case as a
whole; (b) the chambers judge "did address herself to all relevant
circumstances"; and (c) that it could not be said that "she erred in
finding the merits equally balanced where the case is one which will ultimately
depend on findings of credibility."

[
65
]

It seems unreasonable, in my opinion, that a
plaintiff, not knowing what comprises the arsenal of the defendant’s case, must
bear the onus to prove the lack of an arguable defence.  The defendant must, as
Mr. Justice Romilly decided, bear the onus to show it has an arguable defence,
and thereafter it is for the plaintiff to tender evidence to demonstrate its
insufficiency.  This accords with the statement of principle in
Fat Mel's

that security will generally be ordered where there is a corporate plaintiff
lacking assets to satisfy costs in order to protect a defendant with an
arguable defence.

Analysis
and Determination:

[
66
]

My review of the cases shows that much depends
on the circumstances of each case, e.g., the nature of the proceedings, the
availability of evidence at an early stage, and whether the defence can be
gleaned from the documents or whether it turns on findings of credibility.  In
some cases, courts have considered the advice of counsel for a party as to the
nature of the defence.  In others, direct evidence from a party contained in an
affidavit is tendered.

[
67
]

It is also clear that a defendant need not prove
its case on a balance of probabilities since that is what it must do at trial.

[
68
]

Having said that, both the timing of its
application and the nature of the evidence that the defendant chooses to put in
the record is in its hands.
Kropp
makes it clear that a chambers judge
may consider all of the circumstances.  For example, if a defendant chooses
only to put in evidence of a statement of its defence without tendering admissible
evidence, especially where such evidence exists, it is open for a chambers
judge to consider the insufficiency of the defendant’s evidence when the
plaintiff responds with direct admissible evidence.

[
69
]

I reject the insurers' submission that it is
sufficient for them to offer a bare assertion of their defence in the affidavit
of a legal assistant.  That affidavit simply states the opinion and
representations of counsel for the insurers.

[
70
]

Here, the insurers denied coverage for fraud on
October 15, 2008 after completing their investigation.  The denial of coverage
was made some seven months before the lawsuit commenced.

[
71
]

While the insurers have shown a reasonable
defence through defence counsel's advice (contained in Ms. Haines’ affidavit),
the plaintiff has responded by:

(a)       tendering direct evidence of its two principals, which not
only denies their involvement in the theft, but offers an explanation to the
contents of Mr. Senez' report;

(b)       showing the uncertainties surrounding the witness
statement of Mr. Madonna, especially his information regarding the colour
and size of the garbage bags, the date and time on which the person placed them
in the recycle bin, the volume of their contents, and the identity of the
gentleman involved; and

(c)        showing the prospect of further uncertainty surrounding
Mr. Madonna's information arising from the lack of disclosure of the two other
witness interviews Mr. Convey had with Mr. Madonna.

[
72
]

The insurers have chosen on their application to
represent what the evidence at trial will show without tendering any of it in
the form of admissible evidence.  Putting the nature of the defence in evidence
through a legal assistant also shields the insurers' position from further
inquiry through cross-examination on affidavit.

[
73
]

This is not a typical case where at an early
stage of the proceeding a solicitor's outline of the defence might suffice
while defence counsel is seeking to assemble the evidence.  Here, the insurers
completed their investigation and denied coverage for fraud.  The insurers have
had their opportunity to gather in and assemble their evidence; if they had not,
their coverage denial would have been premature.

[
74
]

The insurers have thus chosen not to tender
direct and admissible evidence in the circumstances of this case.  Based on the
evidence tendered by the plaintiff, I conclude that an arguable defence has not
been made out.

[
75
]

Should I be incorrect, so that the mere
statement by the legal assistant of the advice of defence counsel is sufficient
to meet the plaintiff’s assertion that there is no arguable defence, I would
exercise my discretion and dismiss their application for security for costs.

[
76
]

The plaintiff has tendered evidence to show that
its current financial predicament and inability to pay an order of costs arises
from the insurers' denial of coverage, as well as from the implications arising
from a denial based on allegations of fraud.

[
77
]

Although the insurers have tendered some evidence
to show that the plaintiff was in a dispute with several creditors prior to the
loss, the dollar amount of these disputes was approximately $33,786.32.  That
amount is minimal in relation to the plaintiff's annual gross sales (sworn to
by Ms. Helgason) of $1,176,663.00 for 2007 and despite the theft, gross sales
of $790,109.44 for 2008 (which is down from the projected sales exceeding $1.17
million).

[
78
]

The insurers also tendered evidence, through the
affidavit of a solicitor with defence counsel's firm, that a lawsuit may be
commenced against the plaintiff in future for approximately $30,000 because the
plaintiff had stopped making payments on a 66-month lease of office equipment (at
approximately $697.76 per month after 26 months).  Yet, there is no indication
whether those payments were stopped prior to or after the theft.

[
79
]

An application for security for costs should not
be used as an instrument of oppression.  That concern is particularly acute
where, as here, the plaintiff's financial situation is (based on the
preponderance of the evidence in the record) tied to the claims in the action:

Grant v. Henderson Development (Canada) Ltd.
,
2003 BCSC 1473
, paras.
11
and 19
.

[
80
]

In
Scotford Electrical et al. v. Blue
Mountain Log Sales
,
2005 BCSC 538
at para.
23
, the Court said that a link
between a corporate plaintiff's financial circumstances and the cause of action
against the defendant entitles the Court to exercise its discretion against an
order for security for costs or to reduce the amount of security ordered:

[W]here a
plaintiff corporation's impecuniosity and the cause of action against the
defendant are linked, the Court may take this into account in deciding whether
to exercise discretion to award security for costs or in determining the amount
of security to award.

[
81
]

In the instant case, the evidence points to the
difficulties experienced by the plaintiff to be due to its insurers' initial
response and ultimately, their denial of coverage.

[
82
]

Mr. Hilliker wrote to counsel for the insurers
on September 12, 2008, advising:

The fact that
you have refused to confirm coverage (because of your investigation into
criminal conduct) is causing problems with the business.  I was contacted by a
supplier who has been asked to extend credit to Split Vision.  He wanted me to
confirm that insurance monies would be paid.

[
83
]

And then again, on October 10, 2008, Mr.
Hilliker wrote to counsel for the insurers, stating:

I’m advised by
Sheila Helgason that their busy season is coming up and that, given the
production delay between placing an order and receiving product, in order to
plan ahead it is vital that they know whether the insurance claim will be
honoured.  In the circumstances I ask that you again draw the urgency of this
situation to the insurer’s attention.

[
84
]

I agree with the submission of counsel for the
plaintiff that there is a specific consideration in this case that makes the
connection between the plaintiff's financial circumstances and its cause of
action an appropriate basis on which to decline an order for security for costs
(rather than merely the basis for ordering a reduced amount of security).
Prior to the commencement of the litigation, the insurers took the position
with their insured, the plaintiff, that it would have to commence litigation in
order to obtain information about why the insurers denied the claim.  The
insurers took that position notwithstanding an insurer’s duty of good faith and
fair dealing, which requires the insurers, at all times, to be "open and
transparent in dealing with an insured" and "to make available for
inspection documents in which an insured could reasonably said to be
interested":
Alexander v. Great West Life Assurance Co.
,
2004 NBQB
285
at paras.
13 and 14
.

[
85
]

It should not be open to insurers to take the
position that they will only disclose documents if their insured sues them and
then turn around and try to put a roadblock in the way of that litigation by
seeking security for costs (all the while having been told by their insured of
the effect of their denial of coverage on the insured's financial position).

[
86
]

In the circumstances, it is my view that the
insurers are, in bringing the security for costs application, seeking to
capitalize on a situation of their own making – one that unfairly impedes the
plaintiff's ability to bring the claim, since it cannot post costs in the
amount of $50,000 as demanded by the insurers.

[
87
]

For these reasons, the application for security
for costs is dismissed, with costs payable forthwith to the plaintiff in any
event of the cause.

The
Application to Cross Examine on Affidavit and Waiver of Privilege

[
88
]

In view of my decision in relation to the
security for costs application, the plaintiff's application to cross-examine
Ms. Haines is moot.  The plaintiff's application was premised on its position
that the security for costs application should be adjourned and that the effect
of Ms. Haines' affidavit results in a waiver of privilege.  Further, the
plaintiff said that it needed to test the insurers' position in connection with
the “no arguable defence” issue.

[
89
]

In the circumstances the defendants are not, in
my view, entitled to their costs in respect of this application.

[
90
]

As for the waiver of privilege issue, the
plaintiff's position is that in seeking to establish a
bona fide
defence
which may arguably succeed - through a second-hand representation to the Court
by defence counsel that there is a meritorious defence as well as the
particulars of the evidence the defendants will lead at trial – solicitor and
client privilege has been waived.  The plaintiff relies on
Murao v.
Blackcomb Skiing Enterprises Limited Partnership
,
2003 BCSC 558
, where the
Court said, at para. 83:

... [A] client
is taken to have waived solicitor-client privilege if her/his counsel swears an
affidavit on their (the client's) behalf on a matter of substance.

[
91
]

In written submissions, counsel for the
plaintiff took the position that before the Court can accept the representation
of defence counsel on the application, it is of "vital importance to the
plaintiff's ability to prosecute its claim”, and “only fair that everything
that was available to defence counsel when he made that representation to the Court
– his file – be available for scrutiny by the Court and by the plaintiff”.

[
92
]

In the instant case, the plaintiff sought the
following orders in its notice of motion:

(a)       the insurers produce for inspection and copying and
deliver to the plaintiff copies of the documents listed in Part III of their
list of documents dated December 7, 2009;

(b)       the plaintiff be at liberty to cross-examine Natasha
Haines on her affidavit sworn November 19, 2009; and

(c)        the application of the insurers for security for costs be
adjourned until the steps set out above had occurred.

[
93
]

In
Casino Tropical Plants Ltd. v. Rentokil
Tropical Plant Services Ltd.
, (1998),
1998 CanLII 3866 (BC SC)
, 55 B.C.L.R. (3d) 233 (S.C.), Mr.
Justice Warren wrote, at para. 16, that when a solicitor "enters the
fray" and provides evidence in the form of an affidavit, his client is
taken to have waived privilege:

Clearly, where
a solicitor enters the fray and provides evidence in the form of affidavit his
client may be taken to have waived the solicitor client privilege.  In my view,
it matters not that this affidavit was sworn under the provisions of a
particular act. Once a party to litigation relies upon the affidavit evidence
of his solicitor, then the privilege is waived[.]

[
94
]

In
Cheung v. 518402 BC Ltd.
,
1999 CanLII 2654 (BC SC)
, [1999]
B.C.J. No. 2415 at para.
19
, Madam Justice Boyd accepted the submission of
counsel that a party cannot use privilege as a sword:

... the underlying
rationale for a deemed or implied waiver of solicitor-client privilege is to
ensure that a party cannot use the privilege as a sword.  In other words, a
party cannot disclose part of a privilege communication which is favourable,
while hiding part of a communication which is unfavourable.  A party cannot use
a solicitor to avoid having to give evidence under oath.

[
95
]

The principle applies equally to an affidavit
sworn on information and belief:
Re Mannix Resources Inc.
,
2004 BCSC
1315
at paras.
17 to 20
.

[
96
]

In
Pacific Concessions, Inc. v. Weir
,

2004 BCSC 1682
at para.
13
, Kirkpatrick J. (as she then was) set out a
statement of principles concerning waiver of solicitor and client privilege.
The first two are germane to the instant application:

A convenient statement of the principles
applicable to waiver of solicitor-client privilege is found in Fraser v.
Houston, [2002] B.C.J. No. 2204,
2002 BCSC 1378
, affirmed [2003] B.C.J. No.
1296,
2003 BCSC 853
, at paragraph
22
:

1.         Solicitor-client privilege should
be interfered with only to the extent necessary to achieve a just result: Descôteaux
v. Mierzwinski,
1982 CanLII 22 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 860.

2.         Waiver
of solicitor-client privilege may occur in the absence of an intention to
waive, where fairness and consistency so require.  Waiver of privilege as to
part of a communication will be held to be waiver as to the entire
communication.  Similarly, where a litigant relies on legal advice as an
element of his claim or defence, the privilege which would otherwise attach to
that advice is lost: S. & K. Processors Ltd. v. Campbell Ave. Herring

Producers
Ltd
.
,
1983 CanLII 407 (BC SC)
, [1983] B.C.J. No. 1499.

[
97
]

Intention to waive privilege may be implied.
Fairness and consistency may also lead to a finding that privilege has been
waived:
Pacific Concessions Inc.
, at para. 16;
S & K Processors;
Fraser v. Houston
at para. 22; and
Stuart Olson Construction Inc. v.
Sawridge Plaza Corp.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 19859 (AB QB)
, 8 C.P.C. (4th) 185 at para.
7
.

[
98
]

According to
Wigmore on Evidence
, (McNaughton
Revision (1961), Vol 8, pp. 635 to 636 (cited in
Pacific Concessions
Inc.
at para. 23):

... There is
always also the objective consideration that when [a person’s] conduct touches
a certain point of disclosure, fairness requires that his privilege shall cease
whether he intended that result or not.  He cannot be allowed, after disclosing
as much as he pleases, to withhold the remainder.

[
99
]

In
Murao
, which involved a claim for
damages arising from a snowboarding accident, the plaintiff's solicitor swore an
affidavit in which he set out statements that the plaintiff made to him
describing the accident.  The description in the affidavit was not consistent
with the plaintiff's version of events.  The defendants brought an application
for disclosure of the solicitor’s file.  Sinclair-Prowse J. allowed the
application, although she limited disclosure to those communications or parts
thereof that were pertinent to the matters raised in the affidavit.

[
100
]

In this case, defence counsel's representations, made through his
legal assistant's affidavit, can only be the product of everything known to him
at the time the representations were made.  It is not possible, on reading the
affidavit, to segregate what that counsel knew was privileged as opposed to
what he knew was not.

[
101
]

I agree with the submission of the plaintiff that in the circumstances
of this case – where the insurers investigated the loss, denied coverage, and
then chose to tender the affidavit of a legal assistant as opposed to a party
itself to represent the merits of the defence to the Court – the insurers must
accept the consequence, which is to make available the contents of defence
counsel's file at the time the representation was made.  To do otherwise, would
be to do precisely what
Wigmore
forbids:  to disclose as much as the
party pleases while withholding the remainder.

[
102
]

In this case, the insurers chose to represent to the Court the
merits of their defence by a position-statement of counsel expressed through a legal
assistant's information and belief, at a time when the insurers had denied
coverage following their investigation.  In disclosing what the insurers'
evidence “will show”, the insurers waived privilege over the information
contained in defence counsel's file at the time the affidavit was sworn.

[
103
]

I reject the insurers' characterization of the legal assistant's
evidence as a description of the "general nature of the claim to assist
the Court."  Her affidavit contains detailed statements, all based on
information and belief, concerning the evidence that will be led at trial.

[
104
]

The insurers submit that all the evidence their lawyer possesses has
been disclosed.  There is no evidence to support that submission, however.
Moreover, it is now clear that two witness interviews conducted by Mr. Convey with
Mr. Madonna have not been disclosed.

[
105
]

The insurers also submit that the waiver, if there is one, is
limited to the conversations between Mr. Neen and Ms. Haines.  I respectfully
disagree.  The effect of the waiver should not be tempered by the fact that Ms.
Haines, as opposed to Mr. Neen, swore the affidavit, thus shielding defence
counsel and his clients from cross-examination.  The purpose of Ms. Haines'
affidavit is very clear:  to represent to the Court the evidence that will be
led to prove the insurers' meritorious defence.  In my opinion, privilege has
been waived over defence counsel's file concerning the matters raised in paras.
10, 11, and 12 of Ms. Haines' affidavit sworn November 19, 2009.

[
106
]

Now that I have ruled on the insurers' security for costs
application, and given that the plaintiff's application for production of
defence counsel's file was to allow for an examination of the no arguable
defence issue, the question is whether the effect of the waiver of privilege
arising from Ms. Haines’ affidavit should result in an order for the production
of defence counsel’s file.

[
107
]

[The insurers rely on
Northland Road Services (Quesnel) Ltd. v.
British Columbia (Minister of Transportation and Highways)
,
2001 BCSC 937
,
for the proposition that an affidavit must be viewed in the context of the
application in which it was filed (so that on the instant applications, the
affidavit was filed only in respect of the security for costs application).

[
108
]

Counsel for the parties did not make full submissions on the issue
arising from
Northland Road Services
.  During the hearing, it was agreed
that further submissions would be made in respect of the disclosure issue, if
necessary, depending on the outcome of the security for costs application.  In
view of my determination concerning waiver of privilege, counsel should make
arrangements to attend before me to provide their submissions concerning the
disclosure of defence counsel’s file.

Summary

[
109
]

To summarize, the insurers' application for security for costs is
dismissed. Costs are payable to the plaintiff forthwith in any event of the
cause in view of the insurers' conduct:  stating that disclosure of documents
would only be provided once litigation is commenced and then seeking to delay
production of those documents following the security for costs application.

[
110
]

The plaintiff's application to cross-examine Ms. Haines on her
affidavit is dismissed; there is no order as to costs.

[
111
]

The plaintiff's application seeking a declaration that solicitor and
client privilege has been waived over Mr. Neen's file up to the time Ms. Haines
swore her affidavit on November 19, 2009 is granted.  The parties are to return
before me to address the effect of that order in the circumstances, in
particular, whether an order should now be made requiring production of Mr.
Neen's file.

[
112
]

Lastly, in view of a brief submission made to me
a few moments ago by Mr. Plunkett, counsel for the insurers on this
application, I grant liberty to the insurers to address the matter of a stay in
respect of my order for costs when the parties return before me, should an
appeal from my decision be taken.

“P. Walker J.”
